intrinsic_value_estimate: About $64 per share base case, $41–95 range. Method: owner earnings (framework §3, brk-letter-1986). The 1988 owner earnings figure is an estimate of $2.35–2.60/share (no 1988 cash flow statement in the packet), against reported EPS of $2.85. Base case: 10% growth for 10 years, then 4% terminal growth, discounted at 10%, gives about $64. If the past roughly repeats (12% growth, 9% discount rate): about $95. Harsh case (8% growth, 12% discount rate): about $41. Affiliate stakes in CCE, CPE and T.C.C. (market value about $1.9–2.3bn at end-1987) are excluded and would add about $5–6/share. Cross-check: the $46.56 price implies only 3.5–6.4% perpetual growth in owner earnings, against 11–13% historical growth.
margin_of_safety: Fails the literal §5 rule: net working capital is about $0.05/share and current assets minus all liabilities are negative, against a $46.56 price (about 5.4x book). Measured instead against the operative standard, a sensible price for an outstanding business (brk-letter-1981#3, brk-letter-1987#18): about 27% below the base-case value of $64, about 51% below the past-repeats value of $95, plus about $5–6/share of uncounted affiliate stakes. The margin disappears only if growth falls to about 8% and owners also require a 12% return. The margin rests on the durability of the moat, not on assets.

key_reasons.reason: High and rising return on equity, earned without leverage or one-off gains
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE about 20% in 1976–83, then 27.2% (1987) and 33% (1988). About 24.6% in 1986 after removing the $375M CCE gain and $180M provisions. Net debt only 15.3% of capital (ar-1987 MD&A). Operating margin on the restated basis rose from 13.7% to 17.8% (1985–87), so the gain is not just from buybacks shrinking equity.

key_reasons.reason: A durable and widening franchise in concentrate, which earns over 95% of operating income
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: 44% of world soft-drink volume, double the nearest competitor (ar-1987). US share above 40% (upi-1989-01-31). 59% fountain share, outselling the nearest rival more than 2-to-1. Consumers forced the return of the original formula as Coca-Cola classic, which became the #1 US soft drink (ar-1986). 63% gross margin on US concentrate. Pricing power shown by Latin America operating income +17% on volume +1% (1988).

key_reasons.reason: Long reinvestment runway with low capital needs
key_reasons.framework_principle: §1 Berkshire acquisition criteria: demonstrated consistent earning power, simple business, little debt (brk-letter-1982; brk-letter-1987#1 on growing while releasing earnings)
key_reasons.evidence: International per-capita consumption 16% of the US level (ar-1986). US per-capita servings 203 to 274 over 1980–87. 1987 cash from operations $1,231M against capex $300M. Soft-drink international operating income/identifiable assets about 52% (ar-1987 Note 16). EPS from continuing operations rose every year from $0.79 (1976) to $2.85 (1988).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced far more than $1 of market value per $1 retained
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: 1982–88: $6.83/share retained (EPS $13.82 less dividends $6.99). Price rose from $11.58 to $46.56, about $5.10 per $1 retained, and still about $2.00 per $1 at the 1981 multiple. Incremental return on retained earnings about 23%, above management's own 12% cost-of-capital hurdle.

key_reasons.reason: Able, owner-oriented management that buys back shares at sensible prices and has walled off its mistakes
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Honest, able management in place; buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: About 69M shares repurchased 1984–88 at an average of about $31, at 12–17x earnings, all below today's price and below the base-case value of $64. Low-return plastics and pasta businesses sold. Entertainment moved into the 49%-owned CPE with 51% distributed to shareholders. Explicit 12% after-tax hurdle. Disclosures include segment returns, currency effects, guarantees and adjusted EPS (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The price asks for less than the record has delivered; no catalyst is needed
key_reasons.framework_principle: §5 as superseded by 'outstanding business at a sensible price' (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3); §6 market eventually confirms business success (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85 and implies 3.5–6.4% perpetual owner-earnings growth against 11–13% historical growth. The stock was flat at $35–40 through 1988 while EPS rose 17%, then caught up. The multiple barely changed (15.7x at end-1987 vs 16.3x now).

key_reasons.reason: Size fits a concentrated position, short of the 40% maximum
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965); §1 hunt 'elephants' (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: Market value about $17bn, so a position over $1bn is about 7% of the company and can be built. The moat makes it unlikely that value changes drastically. Sized below 40% because there is no asset margin of safety, currency helped 1986–88 results (key currencies +27%, +16%, +10%), and the 1988 cash flow statement is not available.

risks: Currency: about 74–77% of operating income is earned outside the US. A stronger dollar would reverse the 1986–88 tailwinds, and constant-currency growth is not given in the packet.
Owner earnings are estimated for 1988; capex has exceeded depreciation by $150–200M a year, and the packet does not split maintenance from growth capex.

Capital allocation could drift back into low-return areas: CPE earned about 5% on a $989M carrying value and its write-downs cut 1988 equity income 57%; CCE earns about 5.8%; there are $394M of contingent guarantees plus $325M of CPE receivables guaranteed.
Debt-funded buybacks and a 35% net debt-to-capital target conflict with the framework's preference for little debt.
Related-party dealings with CCE (discretionary concentrate pricing, co-op advertising, bottlers resold at carrying value, $415M of gains from selling bottler stock) could flatter reported earnings.
Promotional tone in the annual reports; character has not been verified by direct acquaintance.
Valuation depends heavily on the discount rate; the long bond yield is not in the packet.
Puerto Rico tax exemption expires in 1995; the inflation (current-cost) earnings gap is not quantified.
Entry near the top of the 52-week range ($35.04–49.12); a patient buyer could get better prices, though the framework does not wait on market forecasts.
what_would_change_my_mind: The 1988 annual report shows owner earnings well below about $2.35/share, or capex mostly spent just to maintain the business rather than grow it.
Constant-currency soft-drink operating income growth turns out to be in the low single digits.
Evidence that concentrate pricing to CCE and other bottlers shifts profit into Coca-Cola's own accounts at the expense of the bottling system's health.
Management announces a large diversifying acquisition outside soft drinks, or issues shares on unfavorable terms.
Share loss to the primary competitor in fountain or US food stores, showing the moat is narrowing.
The long government bond yield is high enough (around 11–12% or more) that the base case falls toward the harsh case.
A sharp price decline with no change in the business would argue for adding up to the 40% framework maximum.
sell_triggers: Lasting damage to the franchise economics: sustained loss of worldwide or US share, or loss of pricing power, with returns on soft-drink assets falling materially.
Management turns hostile to owners: value-destroying share issuance (brk-letter-1982#17), repeated diversification into low-return businesses, or loss of candor in reporting.
Leverage moves well beyond the 35% net debt-to-capital ceiling to fund non-core uses.

Default is a permanent holding (§8, brk-letter-1987#18); price alone is not a sell trigger unless the market value far exceeds any reasonable estimate of intrinsic value and the capital has a clearly better use.
